title: The Monthly Dispatch - Whats New in Learning Science - March 2026
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Monthly curated synthesis of recent learning science research. Covers spacing and retrieval practice in STEM courses, testing versus restudy strategies in high-stakes contexts, engagement measurement validation, seductive details in instruction, reading comprehension strategy effects, shared language systems between reading and writing, charisma myths in teaching, controlling instruction effects on motivation, ADHD and sleep quality relationships, early fraction understanding trajectories, AI amplification of the Matthew Effect, smartphone notification disruption, machine learning and self-dialogue, AI versus human art detection, and AI effectiveness in higher education.
points: Spacing benefits in real STEM courses are small and highly variable, requiring context-specific implementation rather than blanket adoption.
Testing with feedback outperforms restudy on transfer tasks in high-stakes preparation; without stakes or feedback, testing loses its advantage.
Engagement is multidimensional; agentic engagement (student voice in instruction) is particularly important but distinct from effort and enjoyment.
Seductive details consistently reduce learning across comprehension and transfer tasks through increased extraneous cognitive load.
Combined instructional approaches (vocabulary plus content plus strategy) produce synergistic effects exceeding any single component.
quotes: In high-stakes contexts, both testing with feedback and restudy produced similar immediate gains. However, only testing with feedback reliably transferred to better performance on the actual course exam days later.
For teachers, the message is uncomfortable but clear: without feedback and without genuine stakes, its benefits largely disappear.
Engagement is not one thing. Students can be thinking deeply, enjoying learning, putting in effort, and actively shaping instruction in different combinations.
A student can look engaged and not be learning, and a student can look disengaged and still encode effectively.
Treating charisma as a rare gift risks discouraging teachers who do not see themselves as naturally entertaining.
Combinations of instructional approaches produced larger effects than individual pedagogies.

Since oral discourse and word-level skills are the foundations supporting both reading and writing domains, strengthening these foundations in the early years provides a double benefit.” Archived from Substack on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
